epistemic-interpretation-of-the-kalman-f.description:
0. Introduction: The State-Space FoundationThe standard starting point for the theory of Kalman Filtering (KF) rests on representing a dynamic system using state-space equations. While the mechanical and multibody systems we analyze are governed by physical laws that are fundamentally continuous in time, modern estimation algorithms are executed on digital hardware using sampled data. Therefore, throughout this text, we will exclusively use the discrete-time formulation.This state-space framework is built upon two coupled mathematical models: The Process Equation: Describes how the internal state of the system evolves from the current time step () to the next (), driven by internal dynamics and external inputs. The Sensor (Observation) Equation: Describes how those hidden internal states project outward into the measurable quantities recorded by our sensors. Together, these equations provide the mathematical architecture to track a system's true trajectory over time. However, a conceptual collision occurs when we transition from pure deterministic mechanics to estimation theory. In filtering, we inject stochastic variables (means, covariances, white noise) into our exact kinematic and dynamic models. If we blindly interpret these statistical terms as purely physical phenomena, we will quickly run into paradoxes—especially when dealing with parameters that are physically constant but simply unknown to us.The following epistemic (knowledge-based) dissertation is a necessary philosophical foundation. It bridges the gap between the exact deterministic reality of a physical system and the probabilistic nature of our mathematical models. Internalizing this perspective is critical for correctly grasping the statistical reasoning that will appear throughout the subsequent chapters. 1. The Ensemble View of the Process Equation In the classical ontological view, this equation is interpreted as governing the statistical ensemble of all possible realizations of a physical experiment. The variables , , and are treated as random variables representing actual physical variations across multiple runs.Here, a single, particular realization of this equation represents one physical reality. In that specific run, and assume concrete, deterministic physical values. However, across different realizations (if the experiment were to be repeated under identical macroscopic conditions), they will take on different values. Consequently, has different "random" values across the ensemble of all realizations. This randomness is driven entirely by true, physical variations across repetitions.The Problem of InferenceThe problem of how to perform inference with this formula begins as soon as we concede: "We don't know the exact initial realization of " "We don't know the exact physical realization of or in our specific experiment" The only things we know are their statistical properties across the physical ensemble, encoded as probability density functions (pdf). For instance: From here, we can begin to make statistical inferences. In the strict ontological view, this statistical description is firmly anchored in physical reality, because the covariances () represent the actual frequency and magnitude of physical fluctuations across real repeated experiments.2. The Epistemic Shift (Knowledge View)While the ensemble view provides a physical basis for probability distributions, we frequently face scenarios where a physical variable is strictly deterministic in reality, but its true value is unknown to us. Leaving aside the realms of quantum and statistical mechanics, this is the realm of classical mechanics that most exactly represents our experience of the physical world as humans.Instead of conflating physical reality and our knowledge using the exact same mathematical variables, we introduce a strict epistemic shift. We acknowledge the true deterministic reality () but map these variables into an epistemic domain to formulate our belief. We do this by prepending a left superscript to denote the epistemic random variable associated with a specific deterministic magnitude.If the underlying state is a deterministic constant in reality, its physical variance is zero. handling-noise-correlation-by-state-augm.description:
The fundamental assumption of the standard Information Kalman Filter framework is that the epistemic uncertainties—specifically the process modeling error and the sensor equation error —are strictly independent, zero-mean white noise sequences. Furthermore, it assumes that the random variables representing these errors are entirely uncorrelated with one another.In complex dynamic systems, this idealization frequently breaks down. We generally categorize these breakdowns into two types of correlation: Spatial Correlation: A statistical dependency across different physical components (e.g., between a process disturbance and a sensor error). Temporal Correlation: A statistical dependency across sequential time steps, either because a noise source has "memory" (colored noise) or because an input noise creates a feedback loop across the update-predict boundary. To maintain the strict optimality of the estimator without breaking the foundational assumptions of the filter, we rely on State Augmentation. By elevating our mathematical ignorance into the state vector, we transform correlated and non-white physical realities back into mathematically standard epistemic problems.Spatial correlation occurs when the physical disturbance pushing the system to its new state is statistically coupled with a sensor error.This correlation happens when a specific disturbance pushing the system to is physically coupled with the sensor error at that exact same instant ().To resolve this, we "store" the current process noise inside the state vector so the filter can explicitly track its cross-covariance. The augmented state vector is defined as:Source 1: The Augmented Prediction ()We inject the "future" process noise into the prediction. Because has not yet occurred at time , it remains strictly uncorrelated with the current sensor noise .Source 2: The Augmented Observation ()The observation matrix expands to accommodate the new state without drawing from the internal noise state:The physical correlation is now handled entirely internally by the cross-covariance blocks of .If the process noise pushing the system from to is correlated with the sensor noise just observed at step , a severe temporal violation occurs. Because the corrected state absorbs via the measurement update, combining this updated state with in the next prediction step creates a hidden cross-covariance.To solve this via state augmentation, we explicitly elevate the sensor noise to an augmented state variable so the filter tracks its correlation with the process noise internally:Source 1: The Augmented Prediction ()We predict the physical state forward. Because is a white noise sequence, its dynamic transition is simply zero, driven entirely by the new draw .The explicit correlation is natively injected into the covariance block, as is now a tracked state:Source 2: The Augmented Observation ()When the new measurement arrives at , the observation matrix maps both the physical state and the new sensor noise state to the reading:(Note: Because $\mathbf{v}{k+1}$ is now fully encapsulated within the state vector , there is no external term in the observation covariance)._A subtle form of temporal correlation emerges when an input signal (treated as a stochastic measurement) drives the system transition () and simultaneously feeds through the sensor equation ().Because the state estimate is corrected using the noisy measurement containing , the updated state becomes mathematically "contaminated" by the input noise. In the next iteration, combining the correlated state and input violates the independence assumption of the prediction step.We stop treating as an external control and internalize it as an augmented stochastic state:Assuming the input follows a random walk driven by white noise , the augmented sources and estimators become:The observation directly uses the augmented state:By internalizing the input, the temporal dependency is resolved. The filter tracks the cross-covariance internally, ensuring optimal de-biasing.While state augmentation successfully solves this temporal dependency, inflating the state vector dimension imposes an penalty during information matrix inversion.
As detailed in the Information Kalman Filter notes, an equivalent optimized approach strictly computes the exact analytical cross-covariance caused by the shared noise, and explicitly injects it into without expanding the state matrices. For real-time estimation, this algebraic injection is often superior."Whiteness" is an idealization. Real epistemic uncertainties often exhibit pure temporal correlation—where our ignorance at step is statistically dependent on our ignorance at (). This typically arises from physical filters acting on underlying stochastic processes: 1st-Order Drift: Slowly varying biases, modeled as a random walk. Higher-Order Oscillations: Structural resonances. Unmodeled inputs: Terrain perturbations or aerodynamic gusts possessing physical memory. To restore optimality, we employ a linear Shaping Filter that transforms pure white noise into the desired "color," appending its internal dynamics to the state vector. Let represent the colored noise state, governed by internal dynamics and mapping into the system via :The Augmented Prediction Estimator:By promoting the noise dynamics to a full state variable, we transform a temporally correlated physical problem back into the mathematically standard white-noise framework. (Note: If the coefficients of or the covariance $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}k}^2$ are state-dependent, they can simply be evaluated dynamically at the current estimate $\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}{\mathbf{x}k}$ within an Iterated or Extended Kalman formulation).Consider a vehicle where the ground profile acts as a dynamic perturbation . This terrain acts as an input to the transition () and creates vibrations that feed through the sensor (). It possesses spatial and temporal correlation, requiring a shaping filter governed by and white noise .When the terrain is unmeasured, we rely entirely on the shaping filter.Prediction ():Observation (): The "Hidden Correlation" is Avoided: Although the measurement relies on the terrain at , the next prediction step is driven by a brand-new, independent white noise draw . Because , the assumptions of the IKF remain perfectly intact. If a laser profiler directly reads the terrain, providing a measurement corrupted by hardware noise , we do not inject this into the prediction step.Prediction (): Remains mathematically identical to Scenario 1, driven strictly by the shaping filter.Stacked Observation (): The profiler reading becomes a direct observation of the new augmented state. Maintaining Independence: The hardware noise enters only during correction. While the updated state becomes correlated with , the subsequent prediction step relies on the true physical terrain variation . Because electronic noise has no physical relationship to the terrain (), the update-predict boundary is cleanly severed. Because state augmentation is structurally additive, we can define a single, unified generalized strategy that simultaneously handles concurrent spatial correlation (via ), temporal dependency (via noisy inputs ), and temporal correlation (via colored noise states ).By stacking all sources of epistemic ignorance into a singular comprehensive state vector, the Information Kalman Filter manages all cross-couplings and dynamics intrinsically.The Unified State Vector:The Unified Prediction Source ():(Note: $\boldsymbol{\epsilon}{\mathbf{u}, k}$ represents the random walk driver for the input, and represents the white noise driving the colored noise dynamics)._The Unified Observation Source ():Assuming we measure both the primary physical state and directly measure the noisy input:While Section 3 establishes the theoretical framework for internalizing temporal correlation via a Shaping Filter (governed by and driven by white noise ), these parameters are rarely known a priori. For physical sensors—whether they act as an observation sequence or a measured input sequence —the temporal correlation is often an artifact of hardware-level low-pass filtering.To maintain the rigorous optimality of the Information Kalman Filter, we must empirically characterize this "colored" epistemic ignorance using an Autoregressive (AR) model and map it to the shaping filter states.The characterization must be performed on the sensor hardware in a purely static, unexcited state over a significantly long temporal sequence of samples. Let this calibration observation history be .The Ergodic Assumption and Experiment Length:The mathematical validity of extracting stochastic parameters from a single time series relies on the assumption of ergodicity—meaning the time average of our single calibration run is strictly equivalent to the ensemble average of infinite identical sensors. To approximate ergodicity, the experiment length must be significantly larger than the longest expected time constant of the hardware filter.Furthermore, during long experiments, MEMS sensors suffer from thermal drift (a slow variation in bias as the electronics heat up). If we simply subtract a constant empirical mean, the remaining signal will contain a slow-moving trend, violating the assumption of strict wide-sense stationarity required for AR modeling.Therefore, the isolation of the purely dynamic epistemic noise requires a rigorous linear detrending over the entire sequence. We model the underlying drift as a linear function of time step :Where and are determined via standard least-squares regression over the sequence . The PACF isolates the direct correlation between and by projecting out the transitive effects of all intermediate lags. Condition for AR(1): If the empirical PACF of the detrended signal falls to zero (within the statistical confidence bounds, typically ) strictly after the first lag (), the hardware filter dynamics are adequately modeled by a 1st-order process. Condition for AR(2) and AR(3): If the PACF remains statistically significant at lag and drops to zero at , the underlying physical filter demands an AR(2) model. A significance up to lag strictly dictates an AR(3) model. Forcing an AR(1) model onto higher-order hardware filters leaves residual temporal correlation within the supposed "white" innovation sequence , violating the fundamental assumptions of the Information Kalman Filter and resulting in a sub-optimal, biased estimator.Depending on the order dictated by the PACF condition, we solve the block Yule-Walker equations to find the optimal Maximum Likelihood estimators for the noise coefficient matrices .For an AR(1) Model:The temporal evolution is defined by a single coefficient matrix. The solution maps the lag-0 and lag-1 autocorrelation matrices directly:For an AR(2) Model:The underlying process is governed by two coefficient matrices (). We determine them by solving the block linear system:For an AR(3) Model:The system expands to incorporate up to lag-3 autocovariance:With the generalized coefficients solved for the required order , the residual sequence represents the true, completely independent white noise that drives the shaping filter.Because represents the fundamental limit of our uncorrelated knowledge (the true "innovation"), its covariance matrix must be analytically explicitly calculated to populate the augmented prediction covariance block:To integrate higher-order AR models into the Kalman framework, the epistemic state vector must be expanded by stacking delayed states. This ensures the Shaping Filter maintains the strict Markov property (where the future state depends strictly only on the current augmented state).Depending on the order , we define the colored noise state , its corresponding Transition Matrix , and its mapping to the observation space :For AR(1):For AR(2):For AR(3):Through this empirical procedure, the unknown parameters of the Shaping Filter have been strictly defined for any required hardware dynamic. The expanded matrix dictates the internal dynamics of the augmented prediction source . The mapping matrix isolates the current time step for the augmented observation source . The innovation variance is injected only into the top-left block corresponding to within the augmented covariance (since the delayed states are deterministic shifts containing no new epistemic uncertainty). By executing this AR() characterization, the non-ideal, temporally correlated sensor sequence is seamlessly mathematically transformed back into the mathematically standard, independent white-noise framework required by the IKF.

non-constant-noise-covariances.html.title: Non Constant Noise Covariances
non-constant-noise-covariances.html.description:
This section expands the Information Kalman Filter (IKF) framework by relaxing the assumption of static covariance matrices. In practice, the epistemic uncertainty—our ignorance regarding the process and measurement—is rarely uniform across the state space or through time. By modeling the process noise covariance and the measurement equation covariance as dynamic functions of the system's context or unknown parameters, we move from a "black-box" noise assumption toward a highly adaptive, "gray-box" epistemic model.In the epistemic view, and are not physical constants of the universe, nor are they rigidly "taped" to a hardware data sheet. Instead, they represent our degree of ignorance regarding the unmodeled dynamics () and the measurement residuals (). They act as the control knobs of the filter's intelligence.If our knowledge about the system's operational environment changes, our mathematical formulation of that ignorance must adapt. We can define deterministic "Epistemic Scheduling Functions" where the covariances are explicit functions of the state estimate, the logged inputs, or time:
State-Dependent Noise: . Context-Dependent Sensor Error: . By making the covariances functions of the state, the filter becomes self-aware; it knows when it is operating in a region of the state space where its mathematical simplifications are weak.When we use functions for the covariance, we can model them in terms of a limited number of parameters, . These parameters then become the subject of optimization using Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE). The following examples illustrate how physical insight motivates this parameterization:Consider an autonomous vehicle traversing varying terrain. The terrain roughness is unmodeled in the deterministic mechanics and therefore manifests as the process noise . As the vehicle increases its velocity , the "impact frequency" with these terrain irregularities increases, which effectively scales the process noise.
The Parameterized Model: We can model this relationship as . The Result: The parameter vector controls how strongly velocity impacts the noise covariance. As velocity increases, the filter "loosens" its reliance on the process model, preventing the estimator from becoming overconfident in a kinematic model that cannot track high-frequency terrain vibrations. In DCM (Direction Cosine Matrix) or quaternion-based attitude estimation, the accelerometer is frequently used to "find" the gravity vector . However, the sensor model is strictly valid only in a quasi-static state.
The Parameterized Model: When the vehicle undergoes linear acceleration, the sensor error naturally increases. We can schedule this contribution to as a parameterized function of the norm difference: . The Result: When the acceleration magnitude deviates from , the filter uses the learned parameters to automatically inflate , effectively "distrusting" the accelerometer for tilt correction until the maneuver concludes. Model errors frequently follow physical patterns. For instance, a discretized model of a decaying pendulum possesses a numerical truncation error that scales with the angular velocity and the discretization time step. By parameterizing as a function of the estimated angular velocity, the algorithm dynamically adjusts its trust in the process equations during high-speed swings.
The Positive-Definite Pitfall: If estimating the components of a covariance matrix directly, standard optimization steps can lead to non-symmetric matrices or negative eigenvalues. It is standard practice to redefine the parameter vector to represent the elements of the Cholesky factor (or matrix square root) , such that . This mathematically guarantees that the reconstructed covariance matrix remains symmetric and positive semi-definite.
To track the state and discover the optimal covariance parameters simultaneously, we start from first principles by defining an augmented state vector:The parameters are modeled as constant or slowly varying, driven by a small artificial process noise ().Because and now depend directly on the augmented state , standard extended Kalman filtering formulas are insufficient. Linearizing these state-dependent covariances introduces additional required correction terms into the prediction and innovation covariance matrices, denoted as and .The resulting optimal estimator (under linearization) is the Generalized Extended Kalman Filter (GEKF), or in its information form, the Generalized Extended Information Kalman Filter (GEIKF). This full augmented filter provides the theoretical foundation for joint estimation by rigorously propagating the cross-correlations ( or ) between the state and the parameters over time.The full augmented GEKF/GEIKF is computationally demanding because it requires propagating a full covariance or information matrix of size and computing complex derivative terms. By applying specific decoupling hypotheses to this unified framework, two well-known practical algorithms emerge naturally as simplifications:The dual filter simplifies the problem by introducing the Decoupling Hypothesis: we set the cross-covariance (or cross-information ) in the state filter. This splits the system into two distinct filters:
The State Filter: Computes the state estimate as if the current parameter estimate were exactly known.
The Parameter Filter: Evaluates the sensitivity of the innovation with respect to the parameters (). It treats the negative innovation as a pseudo-measurement to update the parameter uncertainty ( or ).
RML takes the decoupling idea one step further by abandoning the propagation of the parameter covariance (or information matrix ) entirely.Instead of a full filter update, the parameter update is replaced by a step-size rule driven by the gradient of the incremental log-likelihood. The RML parameter update becomes:where is a scalar step size (Stochastic Gradient Descent). Alternatively, to incorporate second-order information (Natural Gradient / Fisher Scoring), the step size is replaced by the accumulated inverse Fisher Information Matrix . RML represents the computationally lightest method in the hierarchy, ideal for high-dimensional or real-time constraints.
A Crucial Unifying Insight: Whether using the full GEIKF, the Dual Filter, or RML, all three methods are fundamentally driven by the exact same innovation vector: . No artificial "zero measurement" is required. The unified perspective demonstrates that the innovation serves natively as the carrier of information for both the state and the covariance parameters.
This chapter serves as a conceptual introduction to parameterizing and estimating noise covariances online. To deepen your understanding of the underlying mechanics, you are invited to study the specific companion documents detailing the full mathematical derivations:
For Covariance-Form Implementation: Review the document GEKF and Unified Online Estimation of State and Covariance Parameters to explore the exact derivation of the and correction terms via the law of total covariance, as well as the treatment of hidden correlations when inputs are noisy. For Information-Form Implementation: Review the document GEIKF and Unified Online Estimation of State and Covariance Parameters for the algebraically elegant, additively structured parameter updates, and an analysis of how parameters become observable through the second-order statistics of the innovations.

observability.html.title: Observability
observability.html.description: Observability is a fundamental concept in control theory and state estimation. It is defined as the ability to determine the state of a system on a given step, given measurements in that and following steps. If a system is observable, it means that by watching its inputs and outputs over a period of time, we can mathematically reconstruct its internal state.For an LTI system, the state and measurement equations are governed by constant matrices (, , , ). The system propagates as follows:State Equation:Measurement Equation:To understand how observability is determined, we can project the measurements forward in time and express them in terms of the initial state : Step : Step : Step : By gathering these sequential measurements into a single column vector, we can separate the terms dependent on the state from the terms dependent on the control inputs :Because the control inputs () are known, we can subtract them from the measurements. This reveals that we can only obtain the part of that projects onto the rows of the observability matrix.For an LTI system of order , the observability matrix is constructed by stacking the products of the measurement matrix and state transition matrix:The Observability Condition: If the rank of the observability matrix is equal to the number of states (), then the system is fully observable at step .In systems where the dynamics change over time (LTV) or are nonlinear, the constant matrices are replaced by time-dependent matrices or Jacobians evaluated at specific time steps (, ).For time-varying systems, the state transition matrices must be cascaded sequentially rather than raised to a power:Important Caveat for Nonlinear Systems:For a system that is not strongly nonlinear, this LTV formulation using linearized matrices (, ) can give a good idea of the observability. However, strictly speaking, it is only a measure of the local observability (observability in the immediate neighborhood of step ).The classical observability matrix provides a fundamental geometric baseline. It dictates whether the measurement axes, propagated through the system dynamics, eventually span the entire state space. This algebraic rank condition is an absolute, non-negotiable barrier: if , the system contains an unobservable subspace. In such cases, no amount of filtering, smoothing, or sensor fusion can recover the states that remain structurally decoupled from the observations.However, while full rank () is a strict mathematical prerequisite, it is frequently insufficient for practical implementation. The classical LTI and LTV formulations implicitly assume perfect state transitions and exact sensor mappings. In complex mechanical systems—such as multibody dynamics subject to unmodeled joint compliances, friction, or rigid-body approximations—this binary view fails to capture the physical reality of the estimation problem.To transition from the ontological question of "Is it observable?" to the epistemic question of "To what degree is it observable?", we must fully reintroduce the stochastic nature of our models.In the presence of equation modeling noise (), sensor uncertainty (, ), and noisy control inputs (), binary observability is replaced by the concept of the Stochastic Observability Gramian. Rather than a simple true/false rank condition, we evaluate the Fisher Information Matrix (FIM) associated with the state given a sequence of future observations.As established in the Two Filter Information Smoother framework, the precision of our state estimate derived from future data is equivalent to the recursive backward propagation of information. The information pulled back from a future step is heavily modulated by the intervening dynamic uncertainty:This epistemic formulation bridges the classical and practical views by strictly matching the algebraic rank, while exposing the functional limitations caused by noise.The aggregated backward Information Matrix, , serves as the exact stochastic counterpart to . Because observations provide exactly zero information about structurally hidden subspaces, the mathematical ranks are strictly equivalent:If , then exactly eigenvalues of will be exactly zero. Consequently, the covariance matrix becomes mathematically undefined (infinite) along those unobservable directions, correctly representing unbounded epistemic ignorance.Why the Eigenspectrum is the Superior Metric:Practical observability is dictated not by the rank, but by the eigenspectrum of the Stochastic Gramian. The process noise acts as a lossy channel for information; the further into the future a measurement occurs, the more its informational value degrades before reaching . A system may be algebraically observable (full rank), but if the eigenvalues of its FIM are infinitesimally small, the corresponding state covariance expands massively. In practice, this renders the state functionally unobservable, buried beneath the noise floor.For strictly nonlinear systems, evaluating the local Jacobians (, ) requires a nominal state trajectory. Because the true state is unknown, we must linearize around our estimated states. However, computing the Stochastic Gramian backwards requires estimates of the state that depend on the Gramian itself, necessitating an iterative approach (an Iterated Extended Information Smoother).1. Initial Forward Pass:We first run a standard forward Extended Information Filter to obtain an initial nominal trajectory of state estimates and their forward information matrices .2. The Backward Pass (Information Accumulation):Using the forward estimates to linearize the Jacobians, we compute the backward variables recursively from down to :3. State Estimation (Smoothing Fusion):We cannot compute the backward state estimate directly as because if the system is unobservable, is singular. Instead, we compute the fully smoothed state by fusing it with the forward pass (which acts as a regularizing prior):4. Iteration and Convergence:The new smoothed trajectory represents our best epistemic belief of the physical states. We now use these improved states as the new linearization points to re-evaluate the Jacobians (, ) and re-run the backward pass. This process iterates until the change in the Stochastic Gramian () or the smoothed states falls below a convergence threshold, yielding the true practical observability of the nonlinear system.A critical limitation of classical linear theory arises when a nonlinear system is evaluated strictly by linearizing it around a single, stable equilibrium point. At this fixed state, the Jacobians (, ) remain constant. If the resulting classical observability matrix is rank-deficient at this point, linear theory strictly declares the system unobservable. However, this conclusion represents a "linearization trap"—it is only true if the system never actually leaves that exact equilibrium state.In the physical reality of a nonlinear system, as the state moves along a dynamic trajectory away from equilibrium, the Jacobians change continuously. This continuous evolution gives the system "richness," effectively rotating the measurement axes within the state space. By scanning the state space from these changing geometric perspectives, the varying Jacobians often couple previously hidden dimensions into the sensor outputs, rendering the system observable in motion even if it was unobservable at rest.The Stochastic Information Gramian naturally captures and quantifies this phenomenon because it evaluates observability over a dynamic trajectory rather than at a static tangency. If we examine the deterministic core of the aggregated backward Information Matrix over steps, it takes the approximate form of a sum of Fisher Information Matrices projected back to the initial time:Because the matrices inside this summation are evaluated at varying states along the trajectory, each term in the sum represents a different geometric projection. Even if an individual term at a specific step is algebraically rank-deficient, a subsequent term evaluated at a different state may possess a row space that covers the previously missing dimensions. Consequently, the aggregated sum can reliably build up to full rank (), mathematically demonstrating how the rich dynamics of the trajectory render the complete state space practically observable.

two-filter-information-smoother.html.title: Two Filter Information Smoother
two-filter-information-smoother.html.description:
In real-time state estimation, a filter provides the best possible estimate at time using only measurements available up to that moment . state-augmentation-in-the-information-ka.title: State Augmentation  in the Information Kalman Filter
state-augmentation-in-the-information-ka.description:
The fundamental architecture of the standard Information Kalman Filter (IKF) relies on a rigid, idealized assumption: the process modeling errors and sensor measurement errors must behave as strictly independent, zero-mean Gaussian white noise sequences. In complex, real-world dynamic systems, this structural idealization routinely breaks down.When facing unmodeled temporal dependencies (colored noise), physical couplings across the update-predict boundary (spatially correlated noise), slowly drifting internal parameters, or completely unknown external inputs, the standard filter loses its optimality and introduces estimation bias.To preserve the elegant, additive structure of the IKF equations without violating their mathematical underpinnings, we can rely on State Augmentation.The methodology elegantly elevates our structural ignorance or deterministic parameter variations directly into the state vector. By promoting a non-ideality into an explicitly tracked state variable, we expand the system's state space. This mathematical transformation maps complex, non-white, or correlated physical realities back into standard, independent white-noise epistemic problems. Once the state is augmented, the core Kalman filter implementation does not change.We typically deploy state augmentation to solve two major classes of estimation problems.Standard Maximum Likelihood (ML) parameter estimation is suited only to the estimation of strictly constant parameters. However, operating complex physical systems frequently involves parameters —such as friction coefficients, sensor biases, or varying gains—that change slowly with time. Similarly, external dynamic inputs acting upon a system may be entirely unknown and unmeasured.The natural solution is to include these parameters into the state vector, resulting in an augmented state:This requires the definition of corresponding stochastic process equations for these parameters:By simultaneously predicting and correcting this augmented state, the filter naturally achieves real-time system identification alongside its standard state estimation.Beyond parameter tracking, state augmentation is the primary mathematical mechanism used to handle structural violations of the white-noise assumption:
Spatial Correlation: If a specific disturbance pushing the system to is physically coupled with the sensor error (), we store the current process noise inside the augmented state vector () so the filter can explicitly track its cross-covariance internally within the state covariance block. Temporal Dependency (Noisy Inputs): When a stochastic input measurement simultaneously drives the plant transition () and feeds through the sensor equation (), the updated state becomes mathematically contaminated. Internalizing the control input as an augmented stochastic state () cleanly severs this feedback loop across the predict-update boundary. Colored Noise: Real epistemic uncertainties often exhibit pure temporal correlation, where our ignorance at step is statistically dependent on our ignorance at . To restore optimality, we employ a linear shaping filter that transforms pure white noise into the desired "color," appending its internal dynamics to the augmented state vector. To complete the augmented process equation , we must choose a stochastic model that accurately mirrors the physical evolution of the parameter . These models are typically formulated as AutoRegressive (AR) processes.In discrete-time stochastic modeling, an AR process of order , denoted as AR(), assumes that the current value of a parameter depends linearly on its previous values, plus a purely uncorrelated white noise innovation :For the vast majority of state augmentation applications, we restrict ourselves to AR(1) models (where the parameter only has 1-step memory). The specific behavior of the parameter is entirely dictated by the magnitude of the coefficient .When we set in an AR(1) model, we obtain the standard Random Walk. It assumes the parameter's drift is driven purely by zero-mean Gaussian white noise:This formulation is mathematically equivalent to the kinematic integration of pure white noise velocity. It is the most ubiquitous model for estimating unknown inputs, wandering biases, or unconstrained external forces.Asymptotic Properties ():
Expected Mean: . The parameter is equally likely to drift in any direction, so its expected value remains the initial condition. Variance: . The variance grows linearly with each time step (). Because the variance grows without bound, the Random Walk is a non-stationary process. The filter will continually expand its search space for this parameter unless regular, high-quality sensor measurements pull the covariance back down.When modeling physical parameters that naturally relax or decay back to a known equilibrium—such as localized actuator friction, thermal states returning to ambient, or structural perturbations—a pure random walk lacks physical fidelity because physical constraints prevent the actual variance from reaching infinity.For these scenarios, we use the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck (OU) process. In discrete time, this is explicitly formulated as a Mean-Reverting AR(1) model, where the autoregressive coefficient is strictly bounded below unity ():By defining (where is a relaxation rate), this AR(1) formulation acts mathematically like a stochastic spring-damper system. The white noise continuously perturbs the parameter, but the transition dynamics continuously pull it back toward the baseline .Asymptotic Properties ():
Expected Mean: . Regardless of the initial condition, the parameter's expected value perfectly converges to the physical equilibrium. Variance: . Because , the variance converges to a finite, steady-state bound. This means the discrete OU process is strictly stationary. Even during prolonged periods of sensor outage (where no measurement updates occur), the augmented state covariance block for will naturally cap out at this physical limit rather than exploding to infinity.If a parameter or unknown input possesses clear underlying momentum (velocity or acceleration trends), forcing a 1st-order model introduces tracking lag. We can expand the parameter tracking space to include its derivative: .Assuming a constant velocity driven by noise:If the sampling time is small enough, this kinematic formulation can be closely mathematically matched by a 2nd-order AR model (AR(2)), substituting the derivative with a discrete backward difference ():This yields a compact state-space block that bypasses the need for explicit derivative states by leveraging delayed time steps:While state augmentation elegantly unifies parameter identification, input estimation, shaping filters, and correlation management into a singular, standard estimation structure, it comes with a definitive computational cost. Expanding the state vector dimension from to imposes an penalty during the matrix inversion required to compute the joint Information Matrix . This computational load must be balanced against the rigorous optimality and physical fidelity it provides to the estimator.
